questions.prompt: One Newton step for minimization does which of the following?
questions.explanation: The quadratic model at the current point uses the value, the gradient, and the Hessian. Its gradient is the true gradient plus the Hessian times the step, so a stationary point of the model solves \(\nabla^2 f(x)\, d = -\nabla f(x)\). A fixed gradient step never consults the Hessian. Setting the Hessian to zero removes the model instead of solving it. A direction orthogonal to the gradient has a zero first-order change, which is not the Newton equation.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x, y) = 2x^2 + y^2 - 8x + 6y\). At \((1, 1)\), what is the second component of the Newton step?
questions.explanation: The gradient is \((4x - 8,\ 2y + 6)\) and the Hessian is diagonal with entries \(4\) and \(2\). At \((1, 1)\) the gradient is \((-4,\ 8)\). The second Newton equation is \(2 d_2 = -8\), so \(d_2 = -4\). The first component is \(1\), and the sum \(-3\) is not the second component. Reporting \(4\) drops the minus sign in the Newton equation. Reporting \(8\) is the second gradient entry, not the step.

questions.prompt: An invertible linear change of coordinates is applied to the variables. Which claim about Newton's method is right?
questions.explanation: If the new variables are an invertible affine image of the old ones, the Newton step computed in the new coordinates maps back to the Newton step in the old coordinates. The quadratic model transforms with the chain rule, and the stationary point of the model transforms with the variables. Steepest descent does not: it depends on the Euclidean length of the gradient, which a stretch changes. Replacing the Hessian by the identity is steepest descent with step length 1, not Newton. Leaving the numeric step untransformed ignores the change of coordinates.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of one Newton iteration for minimization in order. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The linear system is built from the gradient and the Hessian, so those have to be evaluated first. The system has to be written before it can be solved. The point moves only after the step is known. Rebuilding the model at the new point is the start of the next iteration, not a step that can be swapped with the solve.

steps: Evaluate the gradient and the Hessian at the current point.

questions.prompt: Which claims about a Newton step for minimization are true?
questions.explanation:
A quadratic equals its own second-order model, so the Newton equation is the exact stationarity condition. An invertible Hessian makes that stationary point unique, and one step reaches it.
• A singular Hessian gives either no solution or infinitely many. It does not determine one step.
• With a positive definite Hessian the directional derivative along \(d = -H^{-1} g\) is \(-g^T H^{-1} g\), which is negative when \(g \ne 0\).
• A negative definite quadratic has a single stationary point, and that point is a maximum. The Newton step still solves for it.
• The directional derivative \(-g^T H^{-1} g\) is zero only in special cases, such as a zero gradient. It is not zero for every symmetric Hessian. At a point where the gradient is \((1, 0)\) and the Hessian is the identity, the step is \((-1, 0)\), and the dot product with the gradient is \(-1\), not \(0\).

questions.prompt: The gradient entries are \(a\) and \(b\), and the Hessian is diagonal with positive entries \(p\) and \(q\). The sum of the two Newton-step components equals
questions.explanation: Each diagonal equation is \(p\) times the first component equals \(-a\), and \(q\) times the second equals \(-b\). The components are \(-a/p\) and \(-b/q\), so their sum is \(-a/p - b/q\). Every declared name appears. Dropping both minus signs climbs the model. Adding \(p\) and \(q\) in the denominator, as in \(-(a+b)/(p+q)\), mixes the two uncoupled equations. Using \(a/p + b/q\) forgets that the right-hand side is the negative gradient.

questions.prompt: A note computes a Newton step for \(f(t) = t^3 - 6t\) at \(t = 2\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: Differentiating \(t^3 - 6t\) gives \(3t^2 - 6\), and at \(t = 2\) that is \(12 - 6 = 6\). Differentiating again gives \(6t\), which equals \(12\) at \(t = 2\). Then \(12 d = -6\), so \(d = -1/2\). The false step replaces \(6t\) by \(6\). That different equation is \(6 d = -6\), so \(d = -1\), not \(-1/2\).
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
steps: Replacing that second derivative by \(6\) gives the same step \(-1/2\).
reasons: The second derivative is \(6t\), so replacing \(12\) by \(6\) changes the step from \(-1/2\) to \(-1\).
The first derivative at \(t = 2\) is not \(6\).
The equation \(12 d = -6\) does not give \(d = -1/2\).

questions.prompt: For \(f(t) = t^3 - 6t\) at \(t = 2\), what is the Newton step \(d\)?
questions.explanation: The derivative is \(3t^2 - 6\), so at \(t = 2\) it equals \(6\). The second derivative is \(6t\), so at \(t = 2\) it equals \(12\). Then \(12 d = -6\) and \(d = -1/2\). Reporting \(1/2\) drops the minus sign. Reporting \(-1\) uses \(6\) in place of \(6t\). Reporting \(1.5\) is the updated point \(2 - 1/2\), not the step. Reporting \(12\) is the second derivative.

questions.prompt: For \(f(t) = -2t^2\) at \(t = 3\), the Newton step lands on a maximizer because
questions.explanation: Here \(f'(t) = -4t\) and \(f''(t) = -4\). At \(t = 3\) the derivative is \(-12\), and \(-4 d = 12\) gives \(d = -3\). The next point is \(0\), where the derivative vanishes. The second derivative is negative everywhere, so that stationary point is a maximum. Newton does not switch to minimization when the curvature is negative. The second derivative is \(-4\), not zero. The step is \(-3\), while the gradient entry is \(-12\).
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.
options: the second derivative is zero, so every point is stationary
the step equals the gradient, which points toward a saddle
the second derivative is negative, and the step solves the stationarity equation exactly
Newton always returns a minimizer, so the landing point minimizes \(f\)

questions.prompt: Near a minimizer whose Hessian is positive definite and Lipschitz, the local error of Newton's method is
questions.explanation: A Lipschitz Hessian makes the remainder of the linear model quadratic in the error. After multiplying by the inverse Hessian, the next error is at most a constant times the square of the current error, once the start is close enough. A fixed fraction of the previous error is a linear rate. The Hessian does not have to be constant for that squared bound; Lipschitz control of its change is enough. A reciprocal of the iteration count is a sublinear pattern, and it is not claimed for every start.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls toward the horizontal axis.
options: the reciprocal of the iteration count, from every starting point
bounded by a constant times the square of the previous error
a fixed fraction of the previous error, with the fraction equal to the condition number
unchanged, because the Hessian is constant only for quadratics

questions.prompt: Let \(f(t) = 3t^2 - 12t\). At \(t = 0\), the Newton step is a descent direction. What is the directional derivative of \(f\) along that step?
questions.explanation: At \(t = 0\), \(f'(t) = 6t - 12 = -12\) and \(f''(t) = 6\). Newton sets \(6d = 12\), so \(d = 2\). The slope along that step is \(f'(0) \cdot d = -24\). A negative product is the descent test. The positive value 24 has the sign flipped. The value \(-12\) is only \(f'(0)\). The value 2 is the step itself.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: When forming the Hessian is too expensive, the method that keeps the Newton linear equation but replaces the Hessian by a matrix built from gradient changes is
questions.explanation: A quasi-Newton iteration stores an approximation of the Hessian, or of its inverse, and updates it from the step and the change in the gradient. The secant equation asks that approximation to act on the step the way the gradient change does. A simplex pivot changes a basis of a linear program. Armijo accepts or rejects a length after a direction exists. Power iteration multiplies by a matrix to find an eigenvector.
